entities.summary:
Hugh of Saint-Cher, O.P. was a French Dominican friar who became a cardinal and noted biblical commentator.

Born in the late 13th century, Hugh rose through the ranks of the Dominican Order to become one of its most influential leaders. In 1245, he was appointed as the Master General of the Dominicans, a position that gave him significant authority over the Order's global network.

As cardinal and biblical commentator, Hugh played a key role in shaping Catholic theology during the tumultuous 13th century. His commentaries on the Bible, which combined rigorous scholarship with devotion to the faith, helped to establish the Dominican Order as a major force in intellectual life.

Despite his prominence, Hugh's legacy is also marked by controversy. His involvement in the Albigensian Crusade, a brutal campaign against Cathars in southern France, has been criticized for its brutality and intolerance. Nevertheless, Hugh remains an important figure in the history of Catholicism, and his contributions to biblical scholarship continue to be studied and debated by scholars today.

The 13th-century context in which Hugh lived was one of great upheaval and change. The rise of nation-states, the spread of Islam, and the Black Death all contributed to a world that was increasingly complex and interconnected. In this environment, Hugh's leadership and scholarship helped to shape the course of history.

Hugh's commitment to his faith was evident in his later life, as he devoted himself to prayer and contemplation in his final years. He died on March 26, 1263, at the age of approximately 80, leaving behind a legacy that continues to inspire scholars and theologians today.
